newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon banks cut pound prime lending rate.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon banks cut pound prime lending rate.

text.p: Lebanon's banks cut the Lebanese pound prime lending rate for the second time this year, reducing it to 16 percent from 18 percent in line with falling t-bill yields, the Banks Association announced on Wednesday.
"The board of directors of the Lebanese Banks Association approved at its Tuesday meeting the lowering of the pound prime rate to 16 percent from 18 percent," the association said in a statement.
The association, which groups 79 of Lebanon's 82 banks, cut the rate to 18 percent from 24 percent in mid-January. Before that it lowered it from 30 percent in January 1996.
The prime rate is the rate that commercial banks charge for loans to their best customers. The member banks of the association do not have to follow the group's recommendations but always do.

The cut brought it approximately into line with yields on one- and two-year treasury bills, making loans to customers as interesting to Lebanese banks as the large t-bill investments they have been making in recent years, bankers said.
The high t-bill investments have been blamed for soaking up liquidity and contributing to last year's slowdown in the economy.
The banks said they hoped the reduction would stimulate economic activity and individual bankers applauded the move.

"The association hopes this continuous lowering of interest rates can help the authorities' efforts to activate the national economy and strengthen the Lebanese pound's role in the economic cycle," the statement said.
"This is a very positive step," a banker told Reuters. "It will encourage lending in Lebanese pounds and hence activate the economy and boost production."

Shadi Hanna, treasurer at Byblos Bank and the president of the Forex Club, told Reuters the reduction of t-bill rates by the central bank was a wise move and the prime rate should fall again if t-bill rates fell further.
"Banks can now lend their prime customers part of their excess liquidity in Lebanese pounds at 16 percent, almost the same rate on the one- and two-year treasury bills," Hanna said.
"This cut will rid us of part of the dollarisation in the economy," he added.
The cut follows a sharp reduction of interest rates on Lebanese pound-denominated t-bills in the past five months.

Yields on three-month, six-month, one-year and two-year maturities have dropped to 13.82 percent, 14.55 percent, 15.20 percent and 16.08 percent respectively from 14.61 percent, 16.92 percent, 17.78 percent and 21.62 percent in November.

The central bank said last month that rates should stabilise around current levels, but they are still falling slowly each week. The bank last month began limiting the amount of three- and six-month bills it awards to private individuals and foreign investors.
